title: Some also exclude the motive or impulsive necessity that God might impose
source_text: XVI. Sed praeter necessitatem quae est a coactione, a materia, vel a sensu, aut a quavis alia naturae determinatione, quaedam necessitas est quae concipitur oriri ab aliqua causa externa, velut ab ipso Deo, sic facultatem ipsam movente atque impellente, ut veram imponat agendi necessitatem, id est, ab agente tollat potestatem aliter agendi; licet qui agit supponatur agere sponte, & non invitus. Quam necessitatem Scholae motivam atque impulsivam vocant. Non desunt autem inter Reformatos, qui hanc quoque necessitatem cum humana libertate pugnare existiment, quique putent cum ea consistere non posse ullam proprie dictam necessitatem, quae in Scholis appellatur necessitas consequentis, opposite ad necessitatem quae consequentiae dicitur.
pass_a_gloss: But besides the necessity which is from coaction, from matter, or from sense, or from any other determination of nature, there is a certain necessity which is conceived to arise from some external cause, as from God himself, so moving and impelling the faculty itself, that he imposes a true necessity of acting, that is, takes away from the agent the power of acting otherwise; although he who acts is supposed to act spontaneously, & not unwilling. Which necessity the Schools call motive and impulsive. But there are not lacking among the Reformed, those who think that this necessity also conflicts with human liberty, and who think that with it there can stand no necessity properly so called, which in the Schools is called necessity of the consequent, in opposition to the necessity which is called of the consequence.
pass_b_english: Beyond the necessity that comes from compulsion, from matter, from sense or from any other settling by nature, there is a necessity thought to come from an outside cause, God himself for instance, moving and driving the faculty in such a way that he lays on it a true necessity of acting. That is, he removes from the agent the power to act otherwise, even though the agent is supposed to act of his own accord and not unwillingly. The schools call this motive or impulsive necessity.

Some among the Reformed think that this necessity too clashes with human freedom. They hold that freedom cannot coexist with any necessity in the proper sense, what the schools call necessity of the consequent, as opposed to necessity of the consequence.

choices.why: The standard scholastic distinction: necessity of the consequent makes the thing itself necessary, necessity of the consequence only makes an inference valid. The paired technical terms are kept.
